EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards celebrates a decade of excellence
article:
The EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) marks its 10-year milestone in 2026, recognising outstanding property developments for their design, innovation, landscape, sustainability and sales performance.

Established in 2017, the awards set out to create a credible benchmark for Singapore’s leading property developers and developments. Over the past decade, EPEA has attracted more than 550 submissions, with 67 developments and 14 developers receiving top accolades.

What excellence means for homebuyers

For homebuyers, the awards provide another reference point when evaluating a property purchase. Beyond location and price, the design and execution of a development can influence the way residents experience their homes.

Thoughtful layouts, well-planned communal spaces and cohesive landscaping can make a difference to everyday living, while integrated sustainability features contribute to a development’s long-term efficiency and appeal.

This year’s EPEA theme, “ Celebrating a Decade of Excellence ”, reflects the awards’ focus on developments that go beyond function and aesthetics.

The emphasis is on creating homes and communal spaces that enhance residents’ quality of life, comfort and convenience, with design and innovation delivering tangible benefits.

A live-work-play environment

In addition to residential properties, the awards recognise offices, industrial developments, retail spaces, hotels and co-living projects, reflecting the diverse roles real estate plays in daily life.

Together, these sectors can create a vibrant live-work-play environment, encompassing places to live and stay, workplaces and destinations for shopping, dining, socialising and recreation.

Excellence takes different forms across property sectors, depending on how spaces are planned, designed, used and experienced.

In residential developments, for instance, this may mean enhancing liveability and the functionality of shared spaces, while offices and retail developments respond to the needs of their occupiers and visitors.

Across these sectors, design, functionality and sustainability contribute to a development’s overall quality, relevance and long-term value.

Recognising developments beyond Singapore

For the first time, the awards will also celebrate exemplary developments in Malaysia and Australia. The introduction of these accolades reflects the interest among Singaporeans in property markets beyond their home country, whether for investment or their own use.

For buyers considering an overseas property, the winning projects offer a useful starting point for exploring the market, understanding what different developments offer and conducting further due diligence. Differences in ownership rules, financing, taxation and ongoing costs remain important considerations, alongside the location and characteristics of each development.

Ten years on, EPEA continues to spotlight developments distinguished by considered design, innovation, landscape and sustainability. These qualities can help homebuyers assess how well a property meets their needs, while offering investors a fuller picture of its appeal and long-term potential.

title: Hong Leong Holdings-TID joint venture submits top bid of $1,755 psf ppr for Orchard Boulevard GLS site
article:
The tender for a Government Land Sale (GLS) site at Orchard Boulevard closed on Oct 29, drawing five bids. A joint venture between Hong Leong Holdings and TID submitted the top bid of $181.86 million, or $1,755 psf per plot ratio (psf ppr), for the residential plot that can yield about 110 units.

Bids received for the Orchard Boulevard GLS site

The joint venture’s bid is 8.3% above the next-highest offer of $167.85 million ($1,620 psf ppr), submitted by Global Resource Construction, the Singapore-listed construction arm of property developer SingHaiyi Group .

The lowest bid, from a consortium led by Macly Group and Roxy-Pacific Holdings, was $139.9 million ($1,350 psf ppr). That is 30% lower than the top offer.

The bids received for the Orchard Boulevard site were within analysts’ expectations of four to five offers with a top bid of $1,650 to $2,050 psf ppr.

The highest bid is also 8.5% more than the $1,617 psf ppr UOL Group and Singapore Land Group (SingLand) paid in 2024 for a nearby plot that is now the site of the 301-unit UpperHouse at Orchard Boulevard . The developers beat three other bidders for the site.

Wong Siew Yieng, head of research and content at PropNex, sees the top bid for the latest Orchard Boulevard site as "a firm one". "It is the third highest land rate for a pure residential GLS plot in the CCR since 2018, after the Peck Hay Road site which was awarded for $1,865 psf ppr in June 2026 and the Bukit Timah Road plot that fetched $1,820 psf ppr in November 2025," she says.

The wide spread in bid prices suggest developers had differing assessments of the site and upcoming supply in the CCR. "Developers are likely to have weighed the several prime GLS sites sold since November 2025 that have yet to be launched," Wong notes. Comprising plots at Bukit Timah Road, Dunearn Road, Holland Plain, Peck Hay Road and River Valley Green (Parcel C), the sites could potentially offer around 1,700 new homes in the region.

Compared to the UpperHouse at Orchard Boulevard plot, the "more manageable" development scale of the latest Orchard Boulevard GSL site may have contributed to developer participation, says Mohan Sandrasegeran, head of research and data analytics at SRI.

Developers were also likely motivated by UpperHouse at Orchard Boulevard's performance. Launched for sale in July 2025, the  luxury residential project moved 162 units (53.8%) on its launch day at an average price of $3,350 psf. Caveats lodged as of Oct 28 show that the project is now 82.7% taken up, with prices averaging $3,405 psf.

"The strong take up at UpperHouse suggests that there remains a pool of buyers willing to commit to new homes in the area, supported by the site's prime location, connectivity and proximity to the Orchard Road shopping and lifestyle belt," Sandrasegeran says.

Mark Yip, CEO of Huttons Asia, adds that UpperHouse at Orchard Boulevard saw a median selling price of $3,668 psf in 3Q2026, which provides "key pricing support" for future projects in the area.

Prime location close to Orchard Road shopping belt

The Orchard Boulevard site measures 37,006 sq ft and has a maximum gross floor area of 103,624 sq ft.

Located at the corner of Orchard Road and Tomlinson Road, the 99-year leasehold plot is surrounded by luxury residential developments such as the 150-unit Cuscaden Residences on Cuscaden Road, the 54-unit Park Nova on Tomlinson Road and the 154-unit Boulevard 88 on Orchard Boulevard.

It is also within walking distance of the Orchard Boulevard MRT Station on the Thomson-East Coast Line — one stop away from the Orchard Road MRT Station, which is an interchange with the North-South line.

"Developers would have been drawn by the site's direct proximity to Orchard Road, Orchard Boulevard MRT station and the sales performance of nearby new recent launches, which provide tangible benchmarks for pricing and absorption," comments Leonard Tay, Knight Frank Singapore's head of reserve.

Basd on the top bid of $1,755 psf ppr, he estimates the future development could launch with average selling prices "in the region of $3,600 psf".

Meanwhile, Tricia Song, CBRE's head of research for Singapore and Southeast Asia, projects launch prices to average around $3,450 to $3,550 psf.

title: Sky Seah on what really makes a property valuable
article:
As a real estate economist, academic and mother, Dr Sky Seah understands why parents are willing to pay a premium for a home near a good school.

She believes that premium will endure as long as proximity improves the chances of admission, parents continue to place a high value on primary education, and households prefer to minimise commuting distances.

Seah, senior lecturer in the Department of Real Estate, National University of Singapore (NUS), views the Ministry of Education’s move to increase the number of places available under Phase 2C of the Primary 1 registration exercise as a positive step towards broadening the socioeconomic composition of popular schools.

However, she doubts it will significantly reduce the premium for homes nearby.

The reason lies in a fundamental economic principle: property prices are determined at the margin.

“The premium really depends on the person who is willing to pay to outbid the other person,” she explains.

As long as there is a sufficiently large pool of buyers with the financial means and willingness to outbid others, Seah believes premiums for sought-after locations will endure.

Looking beyond the freehold premium

In Singapore’s property market, freehold homes have long commanded a premium over their 99-year leasehold counterparts, especially in the traditional prime districts of 9, 10 and 11.

Yet the strong sales of two recent 99-year leasehold condo launches at River Valley Green underscore the appeal of newer leasehold homes, even in prime districts.

In August 2025, Wing Tai Holdings launched the 524-unit River Green , selling 88% of its units over the launch weekend at an average price of $3,130 psf.

In March this year, GuocoLand launched the 455-unit River Modern , with 410 units (90%) snapped up at an average price of $3,226 psf on its opening weekend. Both projects are 95% sold to date.

In addition to being at the doorstep of Great World MRT Station on the Thomson-East Coast Line, these 99-year condos offer a greater value proposition in terms of design, layout and efficiency of the units, says Seah.

“They are also likely to be more energy-efficient and offer modern amenities that meet the evolving expectations of today’s discerning buyers.”

By comparison, older freehold condos in the same neighbourhood may offer larger units, but their layouts and interiors could be dated, facilities more limited and maintenance costs higher.

“Purchasing an older, less efficient unit entails an opportunity cost for both investors and owner-occupiers alike, as physical deterioration and functional obsolescence may lead to higher maintenance costs, reduced rental competitiveness, and diminished quality of life when compared to newer alternatives,” says Seah.

She believes the appeal of newer 99-year leasehold developments reflects the difference between paying a premium for perpetual ownership and paying for the quality of the home itself.

Owners who continue holding ageing properties may also tie up capital that could otherwise be redeployed into newer homes offering a better living environment, she adds.

This does not mean freehold tenure has lost its appeal. Rather, Seah believes buyers are increasingly weighing the benefits of perpetual ownership against factors such as connectivity, efficient layouts, amenities and overall liveability.

Renewal through collective sales

The growing obsolescence of older private residential developments could also prompt more owners to consider collective sales as a means of rejuvenating established neighbourhoods.

“I expect that more people will be thinking about collective sales,” says Seah.

On Sept 8, Parliament passed a Bill to lower the consent thresholds for collective sales of older developments, potentially making redevelopment easier once the changes take effect.

However, Seah points out that individual owners’ circumstances can still complicate collective sales.

In the prime districts, some foreign owners who bought their properties before successive cooling measures took effect may be reluctant to sell, as purchasing a replacement home could expose them to the 60% additional buyer’s stamp duty.

Thus, while redevelopment may make economic sense, securing agreement among owners remains a challenge.

Smaller homes driven by affordability

While newer homes may offer more efficient layouts and modern amenities, Seah believes their increasingly compact sizes reflect another reality of Singapore’s housing market: affordability.

“Space is a normal good,” she says. “The more you can afford, the larger a place you will want.”

In economic terms, a normal good is one for which demand generally increases as income rises. Applied to housing, this suggests that buyers who can afford more space will generally prefer a larger home.

Developers have increasingly turned to smaller units and more efficient layouts to keep overall purchase prices within buyers’ budgets.

Demographic changes — including smaller families, more single-person households and couples without children — have contributed to demand for compact apartments. But Seah believes affordability plays a bigger role.

“I think it is primarily due to budgetary constraints that people have opted for smaller units,” she says.

A flattening price gradient

Beyond the size and design of individual homes, Seah believes that improved transport connectivity is reshaping how buyers value residential locations across Singapore.

The nation remains largely a monocentric city, with major employment centres, established amenities and key transportation hubs concentrated around the city centre, she explains.

This has historically created a price gradient, with homes closer to the city commanding higher prices than those farther away.

However, Seah believes this gradient is flattening as Singapore’s MRT network expands, particularly with the progressive opening of the Thomson-East Coast Line.

The decentralisation of employment to regional hubs and improvements in suburban amenities are also contributing to this shift.

At Bayshore, the 515-unit Vela Bay , which fronts Bayshore MRT Station on the Thomson-East Coast Line, illustrates the appeal of well-connected suburban locations.

Developer SingHaiyi sold 72% of the units at an average price of $2,886 psf at launch in April, setting a new price benchmark for the neighbourhood.

Recent Government Land Sale (GLS) tenders also illustrate the changing price dynamics.

The New Upper Changi Road site, opposite Bedok Mall and the integrated transport hub in the Outside Central Region, attracted a top bid of $1,537 psf per plot ratio (ppr).

Meanwhile, the Lorong Puntong site in the Bishan-Upper Thomson area of the Rest of Central Region (RCR) fetched $1,612 psf ppr.

Both exceeded the $1,243 psf ppr achieved for a prime residential site at Marina Gardens Lane, located in the RCR and fronting Gardens by the Bay. It is also a short walk to the Marina South MRT Station.

While individual land bids reflect site-specific considerations, Seah sees the strong pricing of these well-connected sites outside the city centre as an indication of the flattening price gradient across Singapore’s residential market.

She views this as a positive development, giving households more choices of desirable neighbourhoods beyond the city centre without necessarily sacrificing convenience.

More housing choices in prime locations

Seah also welcomes government efforts to create more diverse housing options in established and prime residential estates such as the former Bukit Timah Turf City and Mount Pleasant.

She believes greater socioeconomic diversity in these neighbourhoods is desirable.

Concentrating wealth in a limited number of districts risks creating residential enclaves where households of similar economic backgrounds live, socialise and send their children to the same schools. More diverse housing options could help counter that tendency, she says.

For Seah, the gradual flattening of Singapore’s residential price gradient reflects a market where improved connectivity, amenities and housing options are making more neighbourhoods desirable places to live.

While sought-after locations will continue to command a premium, buyers increasingly have more choices about where — and how — they want to live.

Dr Sky Seah is a judge at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026

title: Desmond Sim on life after Realion: Lessons from football, music and real estate
article:
Six years ago, a friend took Desmond Sim to a shrine in Kamakura, about an hour south of Tokyo. Known as Zeniarai Benten, it sits in a cave by the side of the road. Visitors walk through a narrow passage built into the rock, which opens into a small valley surrounded by steep cliffs.

At the shrine, visitors wash coins and paper money in sacred spring water to symbolise a doubling of wealth. Sim was in Japan for the Fuji Rock music festival.

Shortly after his return, he was approached to lead ETC (formerly Edmund Tie & Co). He took over as CEO in July 2021.

He returned to the shrine two years ago, while in Japan for the Summer Sonic festival, and performed the same ritual. In February 2025, he became group CEO of Realion Group, the holding company of ETC and OrangeTee.

Following the announcement of his departure from Realion on Sept 17, Sim went to Japan for several indie concerts, including Belle and Sebastian’s 30th-anniversary tour in Tokyo. He has followed the Scottish band since the 1990s.

During the trip, he made sure he visited the shrine in Kamakura and repeated the money-washing ritual. The following morning, he received two prospective job offers, with a third lined up. “I’m not particularly superstitious, but the coincidence was too compelling to ignore,” says Sim.

‘A complete circle’

Sim turned 52 on Oct 3. The number is significant, he says. “It represents a full deck of cards, and there are 52 weeks in a year. I call it a complete circle.”

It felt like the right time to take stock. He and Realion management, he says, were no longer heading in the same direction. Being CEO was a great opportunity, but Sim felt he had become a “glorified human resource person, solving other people’s problems”.

Every job, he acknowledges, involves things one may not enjoy. “But when they outnumber the things you enjoy doing, that’s when you start to think perhaps it’s time to go.”

He is not retiring, though. “I still need a job to service the mortgage on my little home,” he quips. He reckons his next role may not come with a C-suite title.

Instead, he wants to return to the kind of work he did for a decade as CBRE’s head of research for Singapore and Southeast Asia: presenting to clients and advising them.

“When you speak to clients, you’re not just imparting your knowledge,” he says. “You are also learning from them, from their reactions and their questions. I’m always very curious, so I enjoyed that interaction, and it’s something that I have really missed.”

This is not the first time he has chosen this path. Earlier in his career, he left a fund management role at Ascendas after less than two years to return to research at JLL.

The football manager

Sim’s biggest culture shock was the move from CBRE to ETC. “CBRE is such a well-oiled MNC. It’s not about the size, it’s about the operations,” he says. ETC, a homegrown firm, worked very differently.

Real estate, he stresses, is a people business. Rather than expecting everyone to think like him, he learnt to adapt to how the team worked and bring people along. “Being a leader is like that,” he says. “You cannot charge ahead, then turn around and realise no one is behind you.”

He likens being a CEO to managing a football club, and that means knowing what each player is good at. “Even if you have 10 Cristiano Ronaldos in your team and they score 20 goals, if you have a lousy goalkeeper and the opponents score 21, you still lose the game,” says Sim. “So it’s about putting the right people in the right positions.”

From CDs to Spotify

The real estate sector has transformed significantly over the past decade. Sim has had a front-row seat, both as CEO of a real estate advisory firm and as a judge on the panel of the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards for the past four years.

Outside property, there is another industry he knows well: music, as both a fan and a musician. In 1987, while still in secondary school, Sim and his friends formed indie-pop band Lilac Saints, with Sim on drums. The band reunited to perform via Zoom during the Covid lockdown, and in January 2023 performed at a reunion concert, Lilac Saints & Friends, at the Esplanade Recital Studio to celebrate 35 years of friendship.

He sees parallels between the two industries, and his own music collection charts the shift. In the 1990s, he began collecting compact discs (CDs), and even went to Ikea to buy racks to store them. At one point, he switched to Sony’s MiniDiscs for their superior sound quality.

Then came streaming. Today, his CDs sit in boxes in a self-storage unit, and he is considering throwing them away. “I can’t even find a CD player to play them anymore,” he laments.

He sees the same shift in how Singaporeans use their homes. “You don’t need a three-bedder that is 2,000 sq ft anymore,” he says. “[Many] people don’t even watch TV in the living room anymore. They are watching Netflix on their tablets in bed.”

‘Stay curious’

Technology has also changed the real estate agency business and how homes are sold. Sim found that out first-hand when he sold his former home at Castle Green condo in Yio Chu Kang in early 2020.

He first contacted the agent who had handled his purchase of the unit, by then a relatively senior hand. The agent came by, photographed the unit and listed it for sale. Two weeks on, there were still no takers.

Sim then turned to a close friend at a property development firm, who recommended a PropNex agent. “The guy came, took a fly-through video, and sold the apartment in three days,” he relates.

With property portals making information easier to access, “even someone sitting in an igloo in Iceland can find out the latest HDB prices in Singapore”, he says. “All you need is WiFi connectivity. You can’t bluff the client anymore.”

As a former head of research, he is frequently asked whether AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude will one day replace researchers and analysts. His answer is no.

“The same set of data can be interpreted in different ways,” he says. “What makes you a key opinion leader is that you take all this data and formulate your own view. Equally important is knowing your audience and how to communicate those insights effectively. That’s what makes a great presenter or adviser.”

People should not fear AI, he adds. “The most important thing is to remain curious. The day you lose the urge to learn, that’s when you will be displaced.”

As for what comes next, Sim is weighing his options. But with his coins already washed at the shrine, he reckons it is only a matter of time before the right opportunity comes along.

Desmond Sim is a judge at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026

title: Another duplex penthouse at Mon Jervois heads to auction, this time at $4.38 mil
article:
A three-bedroom duplex penthouse at Mon Jervois , a 99-year leasehold luxury condo in District 10, went under the hammer at SRI’s auction on Oct 28. The 2,368 sq ft property was offered via an owner’s sale with a guide price of $4.38 million, or $1,850 psf.

Caveats lodged show that the fifth-floor unit was previously purchased for $4.36 million ($1,841 psf) in September 2022.

The penthouse’s lower level comprises a living and dining area that opens out to a balcony, alongside separate dry and wet kitchens. There is also a junior master bedroom with an en suite bathroom, as well as a common room.

Meanwhile, the upper level houses the master bedroom and a roof terrace. Both the master and junior master bedrooms come with private balconies.

Mok Sze Sze, managing partner of SRI Auction, says the development offers a “tranquil, low-density living environment”. She expects the property to garner interest from homebuyers seeking spacious homes.

This is the second penthouse at Mon Jervois to go under the hammer this year. In September, a larger 2,626 sq ft duplex penthouse at the development was put up for auction by Knight Frank at a guide price of $4.83 million ($1,839 psf).

The property did not sell at auction and was withdrawn. However, it remains available for purchase by private treaty and is currently listed at a lower price of $4.6 million ($1,752 psf).

Located along a cul-de-sac on Jervois Road, just off River Valley Road, Mon Jervois is a 109-unit condo that was completed in 2016. Its five low-rise blocks feature one- to four-bedroom units ranging from 614 to 1,905 sq ft. There are also two- to four-bedroom penthouses sized between 1,475 and 3,003 sq ft.

It is within a 1km radius of Gan Eng Seng Primary School and Alexandra Primary School, while River Valley Primary School, Radin Mas Primary School and Queenstown Primary School are 2km away.

Mon Jervois has recorded just three resale transactions this year.

URA caveats show that the most recent resale deal at the development occurred on May 8, when a 624 sq ft one-bedder on the first floor fetched $1.23 million, or $1,968 psf.

Prior to that, a smaller 614 sq ft, one-bedroom unit was sold for $970,000 ($1,581 psf) on March 17.

The last recorded sale of a three-bedroom duplex penthouse at the development was in November 2022, when a 2,368 sq ft unit fetched about $3.79 million ($1,600 psf).

title: Resale of duplex five-bedder scores $3.58 mil profit at District 10's Tomlinson Heights
article:
A duplex five-bedder at Tomlinson Heights in District 10 was the most profitable condo resale transaction during the week of Oct 13 to 20.

The seller of the 4,047 sq ft unit on the fifth floor netted a profit of around $3.58 million (31.9%) when it fetched $14.8 million ($3,657 psf) on Oct 15. It was purchased for $11.22 million ($2,773 psf) in May 2011, resulting in an annualised gain of 1.8% over a holding period of more than 15 years.

Despite the seven-figure profit, it is still far below the condo’s all-time record gain of $4.7 million from a 2022 deal. That transaction involved a 4,951 sq ft duplex penthouse that changed hands for $23 million after it had been purchased for $18.3 million in June 2011.

Tomlinson Heights is a 70-unit boutique condo located on Tomlinson Road, off Paterson Road. Completed in 2014, the freehold development comprises a single residential tower housing three- and five-bedders measuring between 2,745 and 4,047 sq ft. It also has a pair of 4,951 sq ft duplex penthouses.

URA data compiled by EdgeProp Research shows that Tomlinson Heights recorded just two other resale deals this year, both of which were profitable. The units, each spanning 2,745 sq ft, posted gains of $800,000 and $2 million.

Another District 10 development, Leedon Residence , ranked second on the week’s list of most profitable condo transactions.

A 2,659 sq ft, four-bedroom unit garnered a profit of about $3.05 million (63.4%) when it was sold on Oct 16 for $7.85 million. The seller had bought the unit for $4.8 million in February 2014. That works out to a gain of 3.9% when annualised over a holding period of nearly 13 years.

The deal ranks as Leedon Residence’s sixth most profitable transaction, based on caveats lodged. The biggest profit stands at $5.2 million, from the resale of a 4,704 sq ft, duplex five-bedder on Feb 23. It changed hands for around $14 million after the owner had purchased it for $8.8 million in February 2017.

Completed in 2015, Leedon Residence is a 381-unit freehold development on Leedon Heights . It features two- to five-bedroom units, including garden suites and sky penthouses, ranging from 1,044 to 8,051 sq ft.

Excluding the Oct 16 and Feb 23 deals, the condo has logged 13 other resale transactions so far this year, all of which were in the black. Those units were sold for between $2.8 million and $14.3 million, netting profits ranging from $387,028 to $3.75 million.

Meanwhile, the steepest loss among condo resales during the week in review involved a four-bedder at Reflections at Keppel Bay .

The transaction left the seller nearly $2.02 million (28.7%) in the red, which translates to an annualised loss of 1.7% over a 19-year holding period. The 2,928 sq ft unit on the first floor was sold for $5.03 million ($1,716 psf) on Oct 16, after it had been bought in August 2007 for $7.04 million ($2,406 psf).

Still, this pales in comparison with the record loss at the District 4 condo. The seller of a 3,993 sq ft four-bedder incurred the largest shortfall of $4.13 million when it changed hands for $5.85 million in April 2022, down from its initial purchase price of $9.98 million.

Reflections at Keppel Bay is a 99-year leasehold development located along Keppel Bay View. Completed in 2011, it houses 1,129 units across one- to four-bedroom layouts, with sizes ranging from 732 to 4,919 sq ft.

Telok Blangah MRT Station is within a 10-minute walk, while retail and lifestyle amenities at VivoCity mall are a five-minute drive away.

title: Freehold project The Draycott tops weekly record price highs with $2,801 psf sale
article:
The Draycott — a freehold development in prime District 10 — led the list of non-landed private residential developments that posted a new psf-price peak during the week of Oct 13 to 20.

The project’s fresh record of $2,801 psf was set with the sale of a 2,637 sq ft three-bedder on the 29th floor for $7.39 million on Oct 16.

That is the first time an apartment at The Draycott has transacted above the $2,800 psf threshold. It surpasses the previous price high of $2,723 psf, established by the resale of another 2,637 sq ft three-bedder for $7.18 million on July 28.

Completed in 1980, The Draycott is one of Singapore’s earliest and most distinctive developments, located on Draycott Park. It comprises a 34-storey, tri-cylindrical tower housing 132 apartments, as well as four-storey blocks with two-bedders and maisonettes.

Resale psf prices at the development have trended steadily upwards over the past decade, according to a tabulation of caveats by EdgeProp Singapore . Its one-year average resale price has risen by more than 30% over the past decade, from $1,731 psf in October 2016 to about $2,345 psf as of October this year.

Coming in second on the list of top project highs for the week is Lentor Modern . The 99-year leasehold development achieved a new price peak of $2,606 psf with the sub-sale of a 1,109 sq ft, three-bedroom apartment for nearly $2.89 million on Oct 14.

The record-breaking sale inches past Lentor Modern’s former record of $2,596 psf, which came from a 732 sq ft two-bedder that fetched $1.9 million earlier this year on May 6.

Located in the Lentor Hills estate, Lentor Modern is an integrated development comprising 605 residential units across three 25-storey towers above a commercial podium. Completed in 2025, it has one- to four-bedroom units measuring between 527 and 1,528 sq ft.

In terms of absolute price, the most expensive transaction at the development thus far is the sub-sale of a 1,528 sq ft four-bedder, which fetched $3.85 million ($2,519 psf) on May 4.

In contrast to the week’s fresh price highs, only one project registered a new psf-price low.

At freehold condo Peak Residence , a 560 sq ft, one-bedroom unit set a new low of $2,189 psf when it changed hands for $1.23 million on Oct 19.

It is below Peak Residence’s previous low of $2,295 psf, which was set when an 829 sq ft two-bedder was purchased from the developer for $1.9 million in February 2023.

Completed last year, the 90-unit boutique project is located on an elevated site along Thomson Road in District 11. Two- and three-bedders, ranging from 775 to 1,087 sq ft, make up the majority of its unit mix. It also has one-bedders measuring between 527 and 560 sq ft, and 10 four-bedroom units spanning 1,389 sq ft each.

The latest deal marks the development’s inaugural resale transaction and its first caveated transaction since 2023. That year, the developer sold 45 units at Peak Residence at an average price of $2,509 psf.

title: Rental income prospects boost Grade A office market in Hong Kong's core districts
article:
The relatively swift recovery of Hong Kong’s Grade A office market has spurred some owners of properties in prime locations to accelerate the listing of their assets, analysts said.

Stanley Poon Chi-ming, managing director at Centaline Commercial, said the number of Grade A office properties for sale in core districts had increased, with the prospect of stable rental income from well-established finance, securities and banking players appealing to some buyers.

“Grade A offices have become the most sought-after asset class within the commercial and retail property sector, with a corresponding rise in the number of interested parties engaging in enquiries and negotiations,” he said. “Some owners say that it is better to sell now, even at a lower price, while there are buyers willing to step in. That’s why they have chosen this moment to offload their properties.”

An office with a gross area of about 2,449 sq ft on a high floor of the Far East Finance Centre in Admiralty was recently put up for sale with an asking price of HK$45 million ($7.36 million), or HK$18,375 psf, according to Midland Commercial.

Last week, the entire top floor of the 79-storey The Center in Central — owned by Shi Jinyu, the president of Giant Mind (China) — was listed for sale through an agency, market sources said.

They said the asking price for the property, which has a gross floor area of about 13,213 sq ft, was HK$400 million, or HK$30,273 psf, but they believed the final price would be much lower.

Shi bought the property for about HK$738 million in 2017, meaning the asking price is about 46% less than what he paid for it.

Poon said the prices of Grade A offices in Hong Kong had fallen by as much as 60% to 70% from their peak.

A study released by JLL on Oct 26 said overall vacancy rates in the Grade A office market had declined for a fifth consecutive month and stood at 12.4% at the end of September — the lowest level since May 2023.

Central recorded the most significant improvement among the major office submarkets, with its vacancy rate declining from 7.8% to 7.2%, mainly driven by leasing demand.

Sam Gourlay, the head of office leasing advisory at JLL in Hong Kong, said the city’s Grade A office market recorded a positive net absorption of 245,800 sq ft last month.

Vacancy rates for top-tier office buildings had continued to decline because leasing activity was focused on facilities in Central, Tsim Sha Tsui and West Kowloon, he added.

Data from Centaline Commercial indicates that the office property market recorded about 293 transactions in the third quarter of this year, up about 26% y-o-y, with total transaction value reaching about HK$6.127 billion, up about 12%.

Poon said that when attractive prices for high-quality properties offered desirable rental yields, some investors were keen to make purchases.

“This is because most Grade A office buildings are held by developers or major landlords as long-term rental assets,” he said. “It is quite rare for them to be subdivided or sold off in parts. Properties with high profiles that are also available for sale are even scarcer.”

Kelvin Li, director at Midland Commercial, said he expected more Grade A office properties would be put on the market.

“Owners may have different reasons for bringing assets to market, including recycling capital, managing financing needs or rebalancing their portfolios,” he said. “However, the recent availability of prime office properties in Central and Admiralty does not necessarily imply a continued flow of heavily discounted assets across the board.”

title: Behind the Sheraton sale: A window into Hong Kong’s new restructuring reality
article:
The HK$2.7 billion ($440 million) sale of two Shimao Group hotels in Hong Kong leaves an estimated HK$1.8 billion shortfall against their secured loans.

Still, receivers managed to squeeze out improved bids in the final stages, with all shortlisted parties improving their offers, says Una Ge, a managing director at AlixPartners who oversaw the sale as a joint receiver.

The deal offers a glimpse into how mainland China’s developer debt crisis is reshaping Hong Kong’s restructuring industry, bringing vastly larger debt burdens, cross-border contagion risks, and increasingly complex creditor syndicates.

Resolving distressed debt in today’s frozen market is no simple matter of selling real estate, Ge says in an interview with the South China Morning Post .

When AlixPartners took over the 1,219-room complex in Tung Chung in June, its mandate was to protect a live hospitality business from liabilities linked to distressed mainland Chinese developer Shimao, while managing a transaction involving more than 1,000 contracts, Ge notes.

Under agreements signed in late October, the Sheraton Hong Kong Tung Chung Hotel and Four Points by Sheraton will be acquired by Oceanfront Hong Kong, which is controlled by Malaysian property developer ParkCity Group.

Shimao initially sought between HK$6 billion and HK$6.5 billion for the assets in 2023, before lowering its expectations to HK$4.5 billion late last year.

The final HK$2.7 billion sale price represents a 40% haircut to the HK$4.5 billion syndicated loan facility — originally led by lenders including HSBC — illustrating the steep concessions banks are making to reduce balance-sheet pressure and limit provisioning.

Preserving operating cash flow was central to the transaction. AlixPartners worked with Marriott International to ensure operational continuity before court orders were formalised, reflecting the reality that hotels are operating businesses rather than passive real estate assets.

“A lot of communication took place before we were formally appointed, and we had the support of the Marriott team,” Ge says. Maintaining “business as usual” was “critical” for prospective buyers and for lenders deciding whether to support the sale.

That operational stability helped preserve buyer conviction, Ge says.

While borrowers in offshore receiverships often dig in their heels and resist creditor enforcement, Ge says Shimao was cooperative from the outset, providing information and agreeing to publicly confirm in its Hong Kong stock exchange disclosures that the hotels would continue operating normally.

The confirmation was important for reassuring customers that existing bookings, including wedding banquets, could proceed as planned, Ge says.

Shimao’s cooperation in the hotel receivership followed its earlier efforts to reduce liabilities through orderly disposals in Hong Kong, including the sale of mortgaged office floors in Central’s landmark skyscraper, The Center.

The legal mechanics were equally challenging and involved far more than transferring ownership of the buildings. “This is effectively an M&A (mergers and acquisitions) deal,” Ge says. “The hotel company has existing contracts and obligations that come with it.”

Working with A&O Shearman and Marriott’s regional M&A team, the receivers drafted two interconditional agreements separating the physical assets from the operating entities. The structure allowed the Malaysian buyer to assume control without inheriting Shimao’s broader corporate debt obligations.

The transaction required novating more than 1,000 commercial agreements and securing consents under Marriott’s long-term management contract.

Because day-to-day operations would remain with the hotel brand, whoever bought the asset “needed to have real confidence in Marriott’s ability to run the hotel”, Ge says.

The tender drew formal interest from buyers across nine markets, including mainland China, Singapore, Malaysia, Japan, Australia, Europe, the Middle East and the US. Following the initial tender, receivers asked shortlisted parties to revise their terms, and all submitted higher offers.

Ge notes that decisions in such processes were not based solely on price, with execution certainty, financing commitments and board approvals also carrying significant weight.

On the ground, the receivers took direct management of the adjoining T Bay shopping mall, renewing retail leases, upgrading signage and launching guest-discount programmes.

“Anything that adds value, we are willing to go the extra mile for,” Ge says, adding that monthly hotel revenue posted y-o-y gains throughout the sale process.

An 18-year restructuring veteran, Ge says that while the legal tools available to advisers remained broadly unchanged, the scale of Chinese developer defaults had expanded the network of offshore stakeholders beyond anything seen in previous cycles.

As for whether commercial property had reached a bottom, Ge observes that prime office leasing in Central had shown initial signs of stabilising, though it remained unclear how quickly improvement could spread to non-core districts.

Capital values, however, remained under pressure. For property owners and lenders weighing whether to hold or sell, Ge says historical acquisition costs should not drive decision-making.

“People tend to anchor on their sunk cost, which is the original investment. But that may not be so relevant when making forward-looking decisions,” she adds.

According to Centaline Property, lenders were increasingly turning to mortgagee sales to recover cash, while office buildings continued to trade at discounts, with some offered at 20% to 25% below original purchase prices.

With lenders increasingly turning to forced sales to recover their money from distressed properties, Ge says a borrower’s willingness to work towards a resolution could influence how lenders approached a distressed situation.

“If banks see that a borrower is genuinely working hard to improve the situation, in my experience, they are more willing to give their support,” she says.

title: UOB prices 38 Marina Collection units from $1,269 psf, below recent Sentosa Cove resales
article:
UOB is selling 38 apartments at Marina Collection in Sentosa Cove at prices starting from $1,269 psf, following a long-running legal dispute involving defaulted housing loans at the development.

The 124-unit Marina Collection is one of 10 luxury condos in the prime 99-year leasehold waterfront residential enclave of Sentosa Cove. Together, they comprise 1,766 units.

As at Oct 27, there had been 62 resale transactions across the 10 developments this year, based on caveats lodged.

Excluding three substantially larger and pricier transactions at Seven Palms Sentosa Cove , including one involving two combined units, the remaining 59 resales averaged $1,672 psf.

The 17 three-bedroom and 21 four-bedroom units now offered for sale at Marina Collection average about $1,340 psf, 20% below the average resale price across Sentosa Cove this year.

“The pricing has been strategically positioned to offer buyers an attractive entry point into Sentosa Cove’s exclusive waterfront residential market,” says Dominic Lee, head of the luxury team and investment sales at PropNex, the sole marketing agent.

“We believe this presents a compelling opportunity for discerning buyers seeking long-term value in one of Singapore’s most prestigious residential enclaves.”

Lee points out that the average price is even lower than the $1,537 psf per plot ratio (ppr) paid for a 99-year leasehold Government Land Sale site at New Upper Changi Road in September. “That’s just for land, and in the suburbs, in the Outside Central Region,” he says.

Marina Collection, by contrast, is located in Sentosa Cove, District 4, within the Core Central Region.

Below market prices

UOB’s starting price is also lower than previous developer promotions in the precinct. Ho Bee Land Limited offered the last 16 units at Turquoise from $1,290 psf in April 2021, while Cityview Place Holdings, an associate company of City Developments Ltd (CDL) , relaunched The Residences at W Singapore Sentosa Cove from $1,648 psf in April 2024.

As at Oct 27, 18 units had changed hands at The Residences at W Singapore Sentosa Cove this year, at prices ranging from $1,783 to $1,985 psf. Meanwhile, three units at Seascape were sold at prices ranging from $1,549 to $2,080 psf.

Two units at Cape Royale , Sentosa Cove’s largest condo with 302 units and its tallest, at 17 to 20 storeys, sold for $1,846 and $2,148 psf.

What’s on offer

Among the 38 Marina Collection units, the three-bedroom apartments range from 1,873 sq ft (without private enclosed space or PES) to 2,099 sq ft (with PES). Asking prices start from $2.588 million ($1,381 psf) to $2.786 million ($1,327 psf).

The four-bedroom condos range from 2,185 sq ft (without PES) to 2,390 sq ft (with PES). They are priced from $2.948 million ($1,349 psf) to $3.11 million ($1,301 psf).

Of the 38 units, 12 are vacant, while the remaining 26 are tenanted, with leases expiring between 4Q2026 and 4Q2028.

According to Lee, the three-bedroom units command monthly rents of $8,400 to $9,000, while the four-bedroom apartments are rented out from $10,500 a month. Based on the asking prices, estimated gross rental yields range from 3.7% to 4.3%. According to Lee, the yields are “extremely attractive”.

After factoring in monthly maintenance charges of $1,734 for three-bedroom units and $1,951 for four-bedroom units, indicative rental yields at Marina Collection would range from 2.9% to 3.5%, before property tax and other expenses.

The units are being sold on an “as is, where is” basis. The preview runs from Nov 6 to 13, with sales bookings scheduled for Nov 14.

Buyers pay a 1% option fee, followed by another 4% upon exercising the option within two weeks. The remaining 95% is payable upon completion within eight weeks. UOB will provide financing of up to 75% of the purchase price.

End of a long legal dispute

The sale follows the conclusion of UOB’s long-running lawsuit against Lippo Marina Collection, the developer of Marina Collection on Cove Drive.

In October 2022, the Appellate Division of the High Court found the developer liable for conspiring with purchasers to mislead UOB into disbursing inflated housing loans for 38 units sold between 2011 and 2013.

According to court documents, the developer offered buyers undisclosed “furniture rebates” of 22% to 34% after property cooling measures slowed sales, while purchase documents reflected higher prices. UOB disbursed about $182 million in housing loans, in some cases exceeding the amounts buyers actually paid for their properties. All 38 buyers subsequently defaulted on their loans.

In July 2025, the High Court awarded UOB $17.7 million in damages. On Aug 24, 2026, the Appellate Division increased the award to $76.1 million. The amount was subsequently corrected to approximately $82.4 million to account for interest that had been omitted.

Launch buyers sell at a loss

Marina Collection was launched by the developer in December 2007, when units sold for $2,636 to $2,881 psf. Prices peaked at $2,912 psf in January 2008, when a 2,185 sq ft, four-bedroom apartment fetched $6.36 million, according to caveats lodged.

Completed in 2011, the development has approximately 79 years remaining on its 99-year lease.

All four units that changed hands at Marina Collection this year were sold at losses of 32% to 46% from their original purchase prices.

The biggest loss involved a 4,725 sq ft penthouse purchased for $12.67 million ($2,681 psf) in January 2008 and sold for $6.8 million ($1,439 psf) in September. The seller incurred a loss of $5.87 million, or 46.3%, after holding the property for almost 19 years.

In early October, a four-bedroom apartment sold for $3.1 million ($1,419 psf), down 43.2% from its $5.46 million ($2,500 psf) purchase price in February 2010.

Two three-bedroom apartments, each measuring 1,873 sq ft, also changed hands this year. One went for $2.8 million ($1,495 psf) in April, while the other went for $2.78 million ($1,484 psf) in June. Their sellers incurred losses of 32% and 43.8%, respectively.

Meanwhile, the developer has continued selling its remaining units and now has just one apartment left: a 3,789 sq ft, four-bedroom duplex penthouse with a private pool, priced at $6.5 million ($1,715 psf). PropNex is also marketing this unit.

Singaporean buyers to dominate

Lee expects Singaporeans and permanent residents (PRs) to account for the majority of buyers, similar to the profile at the relaunch of The Residences at W Singapore Sentosa Cove in April 2024.

Cityview Place Holdings reported that Singaporeans and PRs accounted for 94% of buyers at the relaunch. The remaining 6% were foreigners from China, France and the US.

The buyer profile for The Residences at W Singapore Sentosa Cove reflects a shift in demand at Sentosa Cove towards local purchasers, particularly after the April 2023 cooling measures raised additional buyer’s stamp duty (ABSD) for foreigners to 60%.

For the 120 Sentosa Cove condo units PropNex has sold since 2016, Singapore citizens and PRs accounted for 75% of buyers, while non-PR buyers made up about 24%, according to the agency’s sales data.

Under Singapore’s free trade agreements, US nationals, as well as nationals and PRs of Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland, enjoy the same ABSD treatment as Singapore citizens. This means qualifying buyers pay no ABSD on their first residential property purchase. US citizens therefore accounted for the largest share of foreign buyers.

Buying to stay

Lee expects most buyers of the UOB units to be owner-occupiers, although some may purchase for investment or as a trophy asset.

Units at Marina Collection overlook the swimming pool, the neighbouring One°15 Marina and the sea beyond. The development is also within walking distance of the waterfront restaurants and lifestyle amenities at Quayside Isle.

“The appeal of Sentosa Cove is that you don’t feel like you’re in Singapore, but in another part of the world,” says Lee.

He adds that Marina Collection offers buyers an attractive entry point into that lifestyle.

Two announcements give investors greater certainty over an established income source, and a sizeable new opportunity in student accommodation -- all in Singapore.

title: StarHub vs Singtel: Which Singapore Telco Is the Better Dividend Stock?
article:
Telco shares are not meant to be exciting.
You can even call it boring.
People pay their phone bills every month, the telco earns a profit, and the dividends should arrive like clockwork.
But is that true for both
StarHub Ltd
(SGX: CC3) and
Singapore Telecommunications Limited
(SGX: Z74), or Singtel?
The duo offer mobile services to Singapore investors.
Both face price wars, rising costs, and heavy network spending.
If that’s the case: which one makes the better
dividend stock
?
For that, we have to dive into the latest financials to see which company has better dividend sustainability and potential long-term capital returns.
StarHub vs Singtel: Two Different Business Models
StarHub primarily serves the Singapore market.
It sells mobile, broadband and pay-TV plans, and also offers companies services like managed IT and cybersecurity.
Consumer plans, which mostly run on monthly bills, brought in about 61% of its service revenue in the six months to 30 June 2026 (1H2026), excluding Ensign.
But average revenue per user is falling, with mobile service revenue down 10.5% year on year and broadband down 8.7% over the same period.
StarHub is targeting S$70 million in yearly cost savings by 2028, with about 10% completed thus far.
Enterprise, the other 39%, is the growth plan.
StarHub’s orderbook is up about 52% year on year (YoY), yet regional enterprise revenue slipped 1.8% to S$290.8 million.
Cybersecurity is a priority, though StarHub — to our knowledge — hasn’t provided any breakdown of its contribution.
Staying Singapore-only is a double-edged sword.
On the upside, it enables StarHub to establish a strong position in a compact market with no currency risk.
But there is nowhere to hide when there is a consumer price war.
In contrast, Singtel is a
diversified
business.
Singtel owns Singtel Singapore and Optus in Australia, plus stakes in associate telcos such as Bharti Airtel in India, AIS in Thailand, and Globe in the Philippines.
Those associates earned S$543 million in the first quarter ending 30 June 2026 (1QFY2027).
The telco’s growth engines these days are data centres alongside enterprise services under Digital InfraCo and NCS, respectively.
When Singapore weakens, Optus and the regional associates can help soften the blow.

Which Telco Has the Stronger Financial Performance?
At first glance, StarHub’s 1H2026 profit of S$258.1 million looks great.
It isn’t.
Most of it is a one-off gain from ending an arrangement with Ensign, which is now an associate.
Without the gain, profit was S$12.4 million.
StarHub expects 2026 EBITDA of just 75% to 80% of last year’s S$403.6 million.
Singtel’s profit is cleaner.
In 1QFY2027, Singtel’s underlying profit rose 21% to S$831 million.
Without a one-off gain, underlying profit still grew 15%.
EBITDA climbed 9% to S$1.08 billion.
Singtel reports cash flow and debt only twice a year, so the latest figures available are for the fiscal year ended 31 March 2026 (FY2026).
It generated S$2.44 billion of
free cash flow
(FCF) in FY2026.
StarHub’s 2025 FCF was negative S$24 million.
Excluding a S$188 million spectrum payment made during that year, FCF would have been S$163.3 million.
In 1H2026, FCF came in at S$40.6 million.
On debt, Singtel’s net debt at the end of FY2026 came in at S$8.7 billion with an interest cover of 19 times.
StarHub’s debt as of 30 June 2026 was S$847.4 million with a net debt to EBITDA of 2.39 times.

title: Google debt-risk gauge rises as earnings revive AI debt jitters
article:
(Oct 29): The cost of insuring against losses on Alphabet Inc’s debt rose on Thursday as its shares plummeted, after disappointing results intensified fears that its massive bet on debt-funded artificial intelligence (AI) spending may fail to pay off.

The price of five-year credit default swaps on Google’s debt, which increases as investor concern grows, rose as much as 5.3 basis points (bps) to 84bps a year, according to ICE Data Services. It’s the biggest increase since Sept 21. Costs also rose for the likes of fellow hyperscaler Meta Platforms Inc and chip company Broadcom Inc.

The Google and YouTube parent reported weaker-than-expected revenue for the third quarter. That includes ad sales, a critical for financing Alphabet’s massive AI investments and which posted its lowest growth in more than a year.

While equity investors could see huge gains if AI investments pay off, debtholders bear the pain if things unravel, according to Gavan Nolan, fixed-income-pricing executive director at S&P Global Market Intelligence. Bond investors are laser-focused on capital spending and when AI revenue will be free cash flow positive, he added.

“In some way credit is telling a bit of a different story than equities when it comes to the tech sector,” Nolan said in an interview.

Trading volume for CDS tied to the 10 largest hyperscalers and chipmakers surged more than eightfold this year to US$176 billion through last week, according to an analysis of trade repository data by Barclays plc credit strategist Jigar Patel. Some of the swaps, like for SpaceX, have only started trading in recent months.

title: Lagarde downplays inflation risk as ECB holds, announces her early exit
article:
(Oct 29): European Central Bank (ECB) president Christine Lagarde played down the danger that inflation will spread beyond energy after news that she will step down early overshadowed Thursday’s decision to leave interest rates untouched.

Lagarde tried to keep her press conference focused on monetary policy, revealing that she and her colleagues discussed and rejected the idea of a hike. Behind that move is a lack of evidence that surging energy prices are triggering things like excessive wage demands and significantly higher inflation expectations.

But with investors leaning towards another quarter-point increase in the deposit rate in December, she left space for further tightening, calling the direction of travel for the ECB “clear”.

“We are very attentive, and at this point in time, we are not seeing risk of second-round effects in addition to what is already included in the projections,” Lagarde told reporters on Thursday in Frankfurt. “We do not see material risk of second-round effects at the moment.”

Market wagers on a rate hike at December’s meeting edged higher, reaching 22 basis points, equivalent to an 88% chance compared with 80% before Thursday’s decision. The euro trimmed a small drop to remain little-changed versus the dollar at US$1.1153.

See also: Race to replace Lagarde begins after she announces leaving ECB in early 2027

Lagarde’s premature departure, on Feb 7, added to concern over energy costs and France. The moves ignited a race between the former central-bank chiefs of Spain and the Netherlands to succeed her in overseeing policy for the eurozone.

On borrowing costs, the ECB is biding its time having hiked twice since the Iran war jolted energy markets. It joins the US Federal Reserve in holding rates steady this week, with the Bank of Japan expected to follow suit on Friday.

Policymakers in Frankfurt are widely expected to raise again in December, when they will get updated economic projections. Rising global bond yields — exacerbated by the market, budgetary and political tensions gripping France — are damping demand.

See also: Bank of Canada raises rates to 2.5%, says more could be needed

“While the full effects of the energy shock are still unfolding, underlying inflation has remained broadly stable so far and wages do not show a material response at this stage,” the ECB said in a statement. “Financing conditions have tightened since the Governing Council’s last meeting, which is likely to weigh on inflation and growth.”

Lagarde, too, zeroed in on gains in core prices, which exclude volatile items like energy and food. “Underlying inflation will probably take a particular standing in the three-prong approach that we apply to our monetary-policy decision,” she said.

The latest rally in energy helped drive the headline gauge of consumer prices up 3.8% in September, with inflation expectations also creeping higher. Oil has jumped by more than 6% since the ECB last set rates, while natural gas hit its highest level in almost four years.

The economy may be starting to feel the pinch: Business momentum and morale are faltering. Third-quarter growth probably slowed to 0.2%, according to a Bloomberg poll of analysts before Eurostat publishes data on Friday. Rate increases contributed to a fall in demand for loans during that period.

“The incoming data suggests that the euro-area economy continued to expand in the third quarter,” Lagarde said, describing risks to the outlook as to the downside. “At the same time, renewed energy-price increases have hit consumer confidence, and higher financing costs are likely to weigh.”

title: Race to replace Lagarde begins after she announces leaving ECB in early 2027
article:
(Oct 29): President Christine Lagarde announced she will leave the European Central Bank (ECB) in early 2027, intensifying the struggle to replace one of the world’s most powerful monetary policymakers.

Lagarde will step down on Feb 7, according to an ECB statement on Thursday. She became the institution’s fourth leader, and the second from France, when she replaced Mario Draghi in 2019. Her term was due to end in October 2027.

“I leave this institution with a sense of good work done, and an ECB that is fit for the future,” Lagarde said in a video message. She is departing to be able to better engage in matters like events in France, according to people familiar with what she told the Governing Council on Thursday.

German bonds and their euro-area peers held small gains. The yield on 10-year German debt remained one basis point lower at 3.36%, while the premium on French bonds held steady at 154 basis points.

Lagarde’s departure sets up one of Europe’s most consequential leadership contests, with the winner to oversee interest rates for the eurozone’s 21 member states and their more than 350 million people.

“To ensure a smooth transition to the next leadership of the ECB, the process for the appointment of her successor will be initiated today (Thursday) and will proceed without delay, with a view to a timely decision by the European Council,” European Council president Antonio Costa said in a statement.

See also: Bank of Canada raises rates to 2.5%, says more could be needed

The Eurogroup will act swiftly to prepare the recommendation for the next ECB president, its head Kyriakos Pierrakakis said in a statement. A decision will be reached by the end of the year, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said.

The move comes at a delicate time for the Frankfurt-based ECB, which is battling elevated inflation caused by the Iran war, against a backdrop of volatile geopolitics, nervy bond markets and massive European spending on defence and infrastructure.

Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos and the Netherlands’ Klaas Knot are vying for Lagarde’s job. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg in October reckon De Cos, a former Bank of Spain chief who currently heads the Bank for International Settlements, is the favourite.

See also: French consumer confidence drops to 13-year low following riots

Talk about Lagarde’s exit had been building. She had repeatedly declined to commit to finishing her eight-year term. Speculation has been rife, meanwhile, that she wants to take over the World Economic Forum, the organiser of the annual Davos gathering.

Lagarde has also indicated she may like to play a role in campaigning for French presidential elections next spring, but ruled out running for the top job. The cryptic remarks have frustrated colleagues at the ECB, with some worrying it’s a bad look for one of the region’s most important economic institutions.

“Throughout its history, the ECB has successfully managed leadership transitions while continuing to fulfil its mandate,” Lagarde said in a memo to staff. “This situation is no different. I know that the ECB will continue to serve Europe with the same dedication during the period ahead.”

The announcement arrives with the US and Iran still failing to strike a lasting peace deal. The ECB lifted borrowing costs in June and September, and markets expect policy to be tightened further.

Bond yields, meanwhile, have spiked around the globe, with investors becoming particularly nervous about public finances in Lagarde’s home country of France. The premium they demand to hold the nation’s 10-year bonds compared with those of Germany recently hit its highest since 2011, leading to speculation of possible ECB intervention.

While Lagarde has argued that projections point to inflation returning towards target around the end of 2027, critics will accuse her of breaking promises to not abandon her post when “there are clouds on the horizon”.

title: Anthropic IPO may spark AI rally as short bets on tech pile up
article:
(Oct 29): Wall Street’s recent risk aversion towards stocks may have created an opening for a sharp rebound, particularly in technology shares, if Anthropic PBC’s planned initial public offering reignites enthusiasm for artificial intelligence.

Investors have reduced their equities exposure to levels broadly in line with historical norms, according to Deutsche Bank. Discretionary investors have cut their exposure to US equities to the lowest in more than a month, while funds that use computer-driven trading strategies have also scaled back. That leaves room for renewed buying if confidence returns.

Hedge funds have gone further, increasingly betting that stocks will fall. Goldman Sachs Group Inc says its hedge fund clients have sold short roughly US$5 worth of stocks for every US$1 in purchases this month. Hedge funds’ use of borrowed money to bet against stocks is now near its highest level in five years, according to the firm’s records.

Those bets could help fuel a rally if stocks take off, forcing investors who wagered on declines to buy shares to close out their positions.

Technology stocks have been hit especially hard, seeing their heaviest two weeks of net selling in more than a decade of Goldman records through Oct 16. Deutsche Bank says investors have sharply reduced their technology holdings since early October, bringing them to a six-month low near levels seen during the Iran war.

The Nasdaq 100 Index has fallen 4.5% since Oct 6 as investor sentiment deteriorated amid a challenging macro backdrop. Brent crude climbed as the war in Iran continued, fuelling worries over higher inflation and elevated interest rates. At the same time, concerns about the sustainability of the AI investment boom have intensified. Comments from cloud-computing provider CoreWeave highlighted the risks of financing AI infrastructure with debt, particularly as interest rates rise.

See also: Mi Material closes at $1.82 on first day of trading; Stabilisation manager bought 1.5 mil shares at IPO price of $1.80

That retreat could make technology shares particularly sensitive to a change in sentiment. A successful Anthropic IPO could renew excitement about AI and encourage investors to return to the sector.

“Investors have been repositioning portfolios as tech and semi leadership has been challenged and we have approached levels where investors just need reassurance that the AI story is still on track,” said Joe Gilbert, portfolio manager at Integrity Asset Management. “The Anthropic IPO will be a critical test for markets once we get past earnings. Similar to the SpaceX IPO, investors will be looking for exposure to a unicorn stock that is one of one — at least until OpenAI comes public — and we believe the demand will be strong.”

Individual investors could also help drive a rebound. From late August to early October, retail investors were buying options betting on stock gains at an unusually high rate compared with those betting on declines. That activity has slowed over the past two weeks, although it remains above average, suggesting investors may have more appetite for buying.

See also: Metasurface to raise $9.82 mil via IPO placement of 18 mil new shares at 54 cents each

“We believe this shows more room for retail investors to add to the AI trade,” John Marshall, a partner at investment firm Carrick Lane, wrote.

SpaceX’s stock market debut offers an example of how a major IPO can attract individual investors. On Friday, June 12, the day the company went public, those investors bought more US stocks than they sold by the largest amount recorded in a single day on Citadel Securities’ platform. The firm handles about 35% of US-listed stock trading by individual investors. Trading in both stocks and options surged.

“There was astronomically large retail participation,” said Scott Rubner, head of equity and equity derivatives strategy at Citadel Securities.

Still, not all investors have been pulling back and dry powder my be running short at long-only funds. Barclays data show that while hedge funds have reduced their bets on rising stock prices, traditional investment funds have continued buying US equities.

Investors have poured about US$340 billion into US stock funds this year, more than three times the roughly US$100 billion typically invested by this point, according to Barclays’ Stefano Pascale. Funds that actively pick stocks now hold less than 1% of their assets in cash, suggesting they have already invested much of the money available to them.

That could limit how much additional buying comes from those investors, even if enthusiasm for AI returns.

title: Google shares drop after 3Q sales miss reignites fears over AI
article:
(Oct 29): Alphabet Inc’s shares fell about 10% in early trading, setting the stock up for its biggest-ever market value wipeout, after the company reported disappointing search and advertising sales that reinforced investor concerns about artificial intelligence’s (AI) threat to its core business.

 

The Google parent reported sales, excluding partner payouts, of US$111.2 billion for the third quarter (3Q), falling short of analysts’ projections. Ad sales from search and other channels — a business line that accounts for roughly half of overall revenue and is critical to financing the massive AI investments — also missed forecasts, growing at the slowest pace in five quarters. 

 

The results and share reaction “show us the margin for error when a hyperscaler spending hundreds of billions on the AI infrastructure buildout” posts disappointing results in its core business, JPMorgan analysts including Doug Anmuth said in a note.

If Alphabet’s premarket share decline holds, it will cut more than US$395 billion from Alphabet’s market value. The shares closed at US$324.89 in New York on Wednesday and have gained 3.8% this year. The company’s performance stood in particularly stark contrast to rival Microsoft Corp, which reported growth in its cloud business that surpassed Wall Street’s expectations while keeping its spending in check, stoking a rally in its stock.

Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said in an earnings call with investors late on Wednesday that the growing popularity of AI Mode, a new tab in Google Search, took a toll on the company’s results. AI queries have “lower monetisation,” Schindler said, though he noted that the company was optimistic and has plans to bring more ads to that part of the search engine.

For years, Google executives have argued that AI chatbots and features won’t cut significantly into its search business. But investors have worried about the impact on the company’s cash cow as consumers turn to rival to ChatGPT, Claude and Google’s own AI features.

The pressure is mounting on Alphabet chief executive officer Sundar Pichai to justify the more than US$1 trillion that Google is facing in future payments on resources such as data centres, computing and energy to power his AI ambitions. “This quarter feels like a moment of truth for Alphabet: Either Pichai and his team fix the way the company monetises AI, or the giant risks losing its leadership in several of its core businesses in the near future,” said Thomas Monteiro, senior analyst at Investing.com.

See also: Alphabet’s revenue miss reignites fears over AI spending binge

“Until Google shows it can charge for AI the way it once charged for search ads,” he said, every capital spending forecast it issues is going to “read less like ambition and more like a bill”.

Google’s sprint to build AI infrastructure for both itself and customers has sent the firm’s capital expenditures soaring to record levels. The firm is working to overhaul popular products such as the search engine, YouTube and Gmail with AI. But those efforts have yet to yield the kind of revenue the investors want to see to justify all the spending.

Google’s overall services revenue totalled US$96.3 billion in 3Q, below estimates for US$98.4 billion. YouTube advertising sales of US$11.2 billion also fell below projections.

See also: Memory stocks lost their shine despite strong earnings

In the meantime, Google’s AI bets are getting even more expensive. By the end of 3Q, Google’s future commitments to buy resources such as computing power and energy totaled US$924 billion. Upcoming obligations such as data-centre leases that haven’t yet commenced hit US$152 billion, bringing the company’s total future obligations to well over US$1 trillion.

For the second quarter in a row, the company posted negative free cash flow, something it had, up until now, never seen since going public.

“Search still generates the bulk of Alphabet’s cash, and two straight quarters of negative free cash flow show the pure AI math isn’t working right now,” said Anders Bylund, contributing tech analyst at the Motley Fool.

Alphabet said in July that capital expenditures will reach as much as US$205 billion this year, more than double what it spent last year. AI requires massive amounts of computing power, and Google is racing to build data centres so it can meet demand for AI from consumers, businesses and its own employees.

Alphabet’s equity investments also weighed on the company’s bottom line. Those stakes posted an US$8.7 billion loss, in large part due to Alphabet’s SpaceX position. That’s a sharp reversal from the gains it saw a year earlier and the windfall in the second quarter that was mainly driven by SpaceX and an investment in a private company that Bloomberg later identified as Anthropic PBC.

Its 3Q net income was US$2.12 a share, falling far below Wall Street’s estimate of US$2.99.

One bright spot in the report was Google Cloud, which is seen as a key gauge of demand for the company’s AI products and hosting services. The division reported sales of US$30.7 billion and profit of US$11.1 billion, surpassing analyst estimates of US$29.1 billion in revenue and US$9.8 billion in profit. Among the unit’s biggest customers are startups such as Anthropic that compete with Google in the AI race.

“Cloud is booming, but many of its best customers are building assistants that are already beating Google with consumers,” Monteiro wrote. “Right now, Alphabet earns more selling AI to its rivals than using it itself, and that gap should keep growing over the next few quarters unless its models change drastically, and quickly.”

Over the past few years, Google has been working to reinvent its search engine for the AI age, trying to keep consumers in the habit of relying on its answers even as chatbots from OpenAI and Anthropic become more popular. The company now delivers AI-generated answers in response to many searches, a shift that has had major implications for businesses that have traditionally relied on the search giant for traffic and advertising revenue.

Google has worked particularly hard on building an edge by generating more personalised responses to questions, leveraging years of information about its users. In recent months, though, the company has fallen behind Anthropic and OpenAI in developing AI coding tools. Google recently released Gemini 4, which it says excels in areas such as coding and cybersecurity, though some employees fear the company has yet to fully catch up.

Hours before its earnings call, Google announced yet another new AI model known as Carbon, a potential answer to the critics who’ve called for the company to speed up the pace of AI development.

“We have more models coming soon,” Pichai told analysts on the call, “including more efficient versions to help developers optimize for speed and cost and to deploy across our billions of users”.

title: Lagarde to leave ECB early, igniting race to replace her

See also: Dutch government plans to cut 25,000 jobs in AI-led overhaul

Lagarde has also indicated she may like to play a role in campaigning for French presidential elections next spring, but ruled out running for the top job. The cryptic remarks have frustrated colleagues at the ECB, with some worrying it’s a bad look for one of the region’s most important economic institutions.

The announcement arrives with the US and Iran still failing to strike a lasting peace deal. The ECB lifted borrowing costs in June and September, and markets expect policy to be tightened further.

Bond yields, meanwhile, have spiked around the globe, with investors becoming particularly nervous about public finances in Lagarde’s home country of France. The premium they demand to hold the nation’s 10-year bonds compared with those of Germany recently hit its highest since 2011, leading to speculation of possible ECB intervention.

title: Aztech rejects US$19.4 mil claim of damages from customer; mulls counter claim
article:
Just as Aztech Global was suffering from target price cuts by analysts, the manufacturer says a customer is alleging breach of contract and is requesting damages of some US$19.4 million to be paid by November 3.

According to Aztech, via a subsidiary, it has been providing certain development, industrialisation and manufacturing services provided to the customer, who was not named.

Aztech says the customer has also claimed that two representatives of its subsidiary, described as key decision makers, are personally liable to the customer on various grounds including, but not limited to misrepresentation, inducing breach of contract and conspiracy.

title: Sembcorp Industries grows Singapore power portfolio with new power plant; to explore energy solutions with DayOne
article:
Sembcorp Industries’s 600MW hydrogen-ready combined-cycle gas turbine (CCGT) power plant on Jurong Island has commenced commercial operations, according to an Oct 28 announcement.

With the new facility, Sembcorp’s total gas-fired and renewables portfolio is now 5.7GW in Singapore, with these assets supporting the growing power demand from Singapore’s data centre and semiconductor sectors. Complementing the generation capacity are more than 2GW of regional renewable energy import opportunities.

“This new capacity strengthens our ability to power Singapore’s AI-driven growth and enhance the nation’s energy resilience,” says Koh Chiap Khiong, CEO of gas and related services for Sembcorp. “Fully contracted under long-term arrangements, the plant will deliver reliable power while supporting Singapore’s longer-term energy transition.”

Separately, Sembcorp also announced that subsidiary Sembcorp Utilities has signed an MoU with DayOne Data Centers. Under the MoU, Sembcorp will serve as DayOne’s technical partner for selected data centre projects, drawing on its capabilities across the energy value chain to evaluate solutions that support their power requirements, including potential opportunities in the region.

With the proliferation of AI adoption, the energy requirements of data centres are becoming increasingly complex. Through the collaboration, Sembcorp and DayOne will explore how different energy solutions can support these projects, from onsite power infrastructure and generation to fuel supply, renewable energy generation, and operations and maintenance services.

“Powering AI will require energy solutions that can keep pace with the scale and pace of data centre growth,” says Koh, who is also CEO of Singapore, Sembcorp. “Our collaboration with DayOne allows us to work together on solutions tailored to the needs of its developments.”
